inline.s: To speak truthfully, the real and the illusory are one substance; sentient beings and Buddhas are not two. Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, bodhi and affliction, all are this original mind, this original nature. There is no need to discriminate, no need to delight or loathe, no need to grasp or reject. This mind is pure and is originally Buddha; it needs not so much as a single dharma. How much idle chatter is there in all this—investigate!
(Recorded from the “Convenient Teachings of Master Xuyun ·
Chan Hall Instructions

blocks.text: In the Beginning There Was No Huatou

inline.s: The ancient patriarchs pointed directly to the human mind and taught that seeing one’s own nature is becoming Buddha. Thus Patriarch Bodhidharma’s settling of the mind, and the Sixth Patriarch’s sole discussion of seeing the nature—could one but take it up directly and wholeheartedly,
there would have been no need for the huatou

. But by the time of the later patriarchs, seeing that the minds of men were no longer simple and honest, unable to settle down body and soul, and given to much scheming and deception, forever counting the jewels of others as treasures of their own, they had no choice but to establish their own gateways and set forth their own modes of instruction, and only then did they cause students to look into the huatou.

blocks.text: The Head of the Word and the Tail of the Word

inline.s: There are many such topics (huatou): for example, “All things return to the One, but to what does the One return?” and “Before my father and mother were born, what was my original face?” and so on. But “Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?” is the most common.
What is meant by huatou? “Hua” (the word) is speech, and “tou” (the head) is what precedes speech. For instance, reciting “Amitābha Buddha” is a word;
before the recitation, that is the huatou
. The so-called huatou is the very moment before a single thought arises.
The moment a single thought arises, it has already become the tail of the word

. This moment before a thought arises is called “non-arising”: without restlessness, without drowsiness, without clinging to stillness, without falling into emptiness—this is called “non-ceasing.” At all times, solely this one thought turns the light back to reflect. This “non-arising and non-ceasing”
is called looking into the huatou
, or attending to the huatou.
To look into the huatou, one must first arouse the doubt

. The doubt is the staff of looking into the huatou. What is meant by the doubt? For example, when one asks who it is that recites the Buddha’s name, everyone knows that it is oneself who recites. But is it recited with the mouth, or is it recited with the mind? If it is recited with the mouth, then when one is asleep the mouth is still present—why then does it not recite? If it is recited with the mind, what does the mind look like? There is nowhere to grasp it, and so one does not understand. Thus, upon the word “who,” one raises a subtle, slight
thought of doubt
, but it should not be coarse; the finer the better. At all times and in all places,
solely attending to and steadying this thought of doubt

, gazing at it continuously like flowing water, without giving rise to a second thought. If the thought of doubt is present, do not stir it; if the thought of doubt is absent, raise it up gently again. When one first applies the mind, one will surely find more strength in stillness than in activity. But one must never give rise to a discriminating mind—do not concern yourself with whether it is effective or not, do not concern yourself with whether it is in activity or in stillness. Just apply your effort with one whole mind
[To look into the huatou, one must first arouse the doubt]
Then how does one arouse the doubt? Elder Master Xuyun said: “Begin by investigating the tail of the word.” In his “Two Letters to Layman Jin Hongshu (

),” Elder Master Xuyun said: “If a beginner applies effort, he cannot but investigate from the tail of the word. For the sentient beings of the Latter Age of the Dharma are thick in obstructions and shallow in wisdom; without beginning from the tail of the word, it is hard to reach the huatou; without applying effort at the place where the conscious mind is, it is hard to realize the mind that is without thought.” In the “Admonitions on Chan Practice,” Elder Master Xuyun said: “If you have not yet seen the huatou (the head, that which precedes the word), and your idle thoughts and drowsiness are many, then you should still look at the word ‘who’ in ‘Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?’ When you have seen it so that idle thoughts and drowsiness are few, and the word ‘who’ can no longer be forgotten, then look at the very place where this single thought arises. When a single thought no longer arises, that is non-arising; to be able to see the non-arising of a single thought is called truly looking into the huatou.”

blocks.text: First Investigate the Tail of the Word

inline.s: Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?”—the four characters place the greatest weight on the single word “who.” The other three characters merely indicate the general matter. For instance, who is it that puts on clothes and eats? Who is it that defecates and urinates? Who is it that gives rise to ignorance? Who is it that knows and is aware? Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, once the word “who” is raised it most easily gives rise to a thought of doubt, without waiting for repeated pondering, conjecture, or deliberate intention. For this reason, the “who” word as huatou is truly a wondrous method of Chan practice.

But this is not taking the word “who” or the four characters “Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?” and reciting them as a Buddha-name, nor is it the pondering and conjecture of seeking out who it is that recites the Buddha’s name and calling that the doubt. There be some
(certain people)

who recite the four characters “Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?” without ever stopping; this is not as meritorious as reciting a single “Amitābha Buddha.” There be others who let their thoughts run wild and search here and there, and call that the doubt—little do they know that the more they think, the more idle thoughts arise, which is like wishing to rise yet falling instead. One must know this.

The doubting thought of a beginner is very coarse, now broken off and now resumed, now familiar and now new. It does not count as the doubt; it may only be called thinking. Gradually, as the wild mind is reined in and the thought can be held a little steady,
then it is called investigating (can)

. Further, as the effort gradually ripens, one later doubts without intending to doubt. One no longer is aware of where one sits, nor does one know of body, mind, or world. Solely the thought of doubt appears before one, unbroken and uninterrupted, and then
this is called the doubt
. In truth, to speak practically—does that earlier stage count as real effort? It is merely beating up idle fancies.
Only when the true doubt
(the genuine doubt—thought after thought, without interruption, investigating toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted)
now appears
—that is the time of true effort.
This is a great pass, where one can very easily run off onto a wrong path

[Guān’ài (a strategic pass)]A strategically vital defile. [This is a great pass]This is a great and dangerous pass. When one’s effort reaches the stage of “doubting without intending to doubt, no longer aware of where one sits, no longer knowing body, mind, or world, solely the thought of doubt appearing before one, unbroken and uninterrupted,” then the following pure and clear states appear. If one cannot handle them properly, one can very easily run off onto a wrong path.

1. At this time one is pure and clear, with boundless ease and well-being. Should one lose awareness and illumination even slightly, one sinks into a state of light drowsiness. Were there a person with clear eyes at one’s side, he would see at a glance that one is dwelling in this realm, and with a single blow of the incense board the clouds and mists would instantly disperse—and many have thereby awakened to the Way.

2. At this time one is pure and clear, empty and hollow. If the doubt has vanished, this is the indifferent state, sitting on a withered-tree crag, or what is called “soaking rocks in cold water.” At this point one must raise it—
to raise is awareness and illumination

. Awareness means not being deluded, and that is wisdom; illumination means not being disturbed, and that is samādhi. Solely this single thought, clear and still, as calm and unmoving, numinously undimmed, constantly aware—like cold fire drawing forth smoke, a single thread stretching on without breaking.
[Solely this single thought]Merely this one thought of awareness and illumination, and nothing else.
When effort has reached this stage, one must possess the diamond (vajra) eye—
no longer raise it

, for raising is placing a head upon a head. Formerly a monk asked the Old Master Zhaozhou: “When not a single thing is brought, what then?” Zhaozhou said: “Put it down.” The monk said: “If not a single thing is brought, what is there to put down?” Zhaozhou said: “If you cannot put it down, take it up and carry it.” This is precisely speaking of this juncture. The scenery within it is like a person drinking water, who knows for himself whether it is warm or cold; it cannot be reached by words. One who has reached this stage naturally understands; one who has not reached this stage gains nothing from being told. As the saying goes, “Meeting a swordsman by the way, one must present a sword; it is not for a poet to offer a poem.”
[When effort has reached this stage]the application of effort reaching

the stage of “solely this single thought, clear and still, as calm and unmoving, numinously undimmed, constantly aware—like cold fire drawing forth smoke, a single thread stretching on without breaking.” [No longer raise it]At this point, although one no longer raises awareness and illumination, the illumination is still present, illumining of itself—this is called silent illumination. Still, it is ever illumining; illumining, it is ever still. Master Dayu’s verse says: “Silent illumination, illumining stillness—above all, do not use force. To become a Buddha and be master, there is no other secret.” This is precisely what is meant by this realm of silent illumination.

blocks.text: The Instructions of the Venerable Grand Master

inline.s: Recorded from
Master Xuyun’s Convenient Instructions
In the thirty-sixth year of the Republic
, during the winter Chan session, I went up to the abbot’s quarters to request instructions.
The Grand Master asked me: “What practice do you use?”
I said: “I also recite the Buddha’s name and also investigate Chan, practicing Chan and Pure Land in tandem.”
He asked: “Since you recite the Buddha’s name, how can you also investigate Chan?”
I said: “When I recite the Buddha’s name, my mind holds the doubt of who it is that is reciting the Buddha’s name; so although I am reciting the Buddha’s name, it is at the same time Chan practice.”

He asked: “Are there idle thoughts?” I answered: “When right mindfulness is raised, delusive thoughts often arise following along behind it. When right mindfulness is set down, then there are no delusive thoughts either—pure and free.”

The Grand Master said: “This purity and freedom are laziness and sloth—soaking rocks in cold water; even cultivating for a thousand years would be a waste. You must surely raise right mindfulness and investigate with fierce vigor, and see through to who it is who is ultimately reciting the Buddha’s name. Only then can you break through. You must apply effort with diligence.”
He asked: “I have heard that, at Zhongnan Mountain, the Grand Master entered samādhi for eighteen days. Did he enter with a mind, or without a mind?”

I answered: “Entering samādhi with a mind, one surely cannot be settled. Entering samādhi without a mind is like a statue of clay or wood. When the mind is held to a single place, nothing is left undone.”
He asked: “I wish to learn from the Grand Master how to enter samādhi; please teach me, Grand Master.”
I answered: “It is impossible without looking into the huatou.”
He asked: “What is called the huatou?”
He answered: “‘Hua’ (the word) is idle thought—one’s own talking to oneself.
In the place where idle thoughts have not yet arisen, observe and watch: see what the original face is. This is called looking into the huatou.

When idle thoughts have already arisen, still raise right mindfulness, and the wrong thought will vanish of itself. If one follows after idle thoughts, sitting in meditation is of no benefit. If one raises right mindfulness but it is not earnest, then the huatou is without strength and the delusive thoughts must arise. Therefore, in applying effort one must be fierce and diligent, as if mourning one’s own parents. An ancient worthy said: ‘Learning the Way is like guarding a walled city; tightly guard the city wall through a whole battle. Without once enduring the cold that pierces the very bone, how could the plum blossom greet the nose with its fragrance?’ (These words the Grand Master would repeat at every session.)
If there are no idle thoughts, then neither is there a huatou. Sitting still with an empty mind, soaking rocks in cold water—even sitting through countless eons brings no benefit.

If one does not investigate Chan, so be it; but once one has resolved to investigate, one must be fierce and diligent, like a single man contending against ten thousand, advancing straight ahead without retreating, not relaxing in the least. Reciting the Buddha’s name is likewise; holding the mantra is likewise. When the thought of birth-and-death is earnest, and each day becomes more pressing than the last, then the effort will make progress.”

blocks.text: Attending to the Huatou and Turning the Hearing Inward to Self-Nature

inline.s: Excerpted from Master Xuyun’s Convenient Instructions · Chan Hall Instructions.

What is meant by huatou? “Hua” (the word) is speech, and “tou” (the head) is what precedes speech. For instance, reciting “Amitābha Buddha” is a word; before the recitation, that is the huatou. The so-called huatou is the very moment before a single thought arises; the moment a single thought arises, it has already become the tail of the word. This moment before a thought arises is called “non-arising”; without restlessness, without drowsiness, without clinging to stillness, without falling into emptiness, it is called “non-ceasing.” At all times, solely this single thought turns the light back to reflect upon this “non-arising and non-ceasing”—this is called looking into the huatou, or attending to the huatou.

[Non-arising and non-ceasing]The “non-arising and non-ceasing” spoken of here means: a single thought does not arise, and the investigation does not cease (without restlessness, without drowsiness, without clinging to stillness, without falling into emptiness). [Restlessness (diāojǔ)]The agitation of mental thought.
Someone asks
(a person asks)
: “How is it evident that the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara’s turning the hearing inward to hear self-nature is Chan practice?”

[Turning the hearing inward to hear self-nature is precisely Chan practice]When Elder Master Xuyun spoke in the “Chan Hall Instructions” about the method of Chan practice, he said: “Though the methods of practice are many, all the Buddhas and patriarchs regard Chan practice as the supreme, wondrous gateway. At the Śūraṅgama assembly, the Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva to select the path of perfect penetration, and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s perfect penetration of the ear faculty was deemed the foremost. When we turn the hearing inward to hear self-nature, that is Chan practice.”
I just
(just now)
said that attending to the huatou means teaching you, at all times, solely this single thought, turning the light back to reflect upon this “non-arising and non-ceasing.”
Turning the hearing inward to hear self-nature also means teaching you, at all times, solely this single thought, turning the hearing inward to hear self-nature.

“Turning” means going against; “non-arising and non-ceasing” is self-nature. Although, when flowing downstream, “hearing” and “illuminating” follow sounds and chase after forms—the hearing not going beyond the sound, the seeing not going beyond the form, with discrimination plainly apparent—yet when one goes against the stream and reversely observes self-nature, not following sounds nor chasing after forms, then it is originally a single pure awareness, and “hearing” and “illuminating” are not two different things. We must know: the so-called attending to the huatou, the so-called turning the hearing inward to hear self-nature, is absolutely not looking with the eyes, nor listening with the ears. Were one to look with the eyes or listen with the ears, that would be following sounds and chasing after forms, being turned by objects, which is called flowing downstream. If solely this single thought dwells in “non-arising and non-ceasing,” not following sounds nor chasing after forms, that is called going against the stream, called attending to the huatou, and also called turning the hearing inward to hear self-nature.

[Turning the hearing inward to hear self-nature]The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: “Turning the hearing inward to hear self-nature, the nature accomplishes the supreme Way.” Regarding turning the hearing inward to hear self-nature, there is a most brilliant passage in the “Essentials of Cultivating the Mind”: “There are many ways of entering the principle; I point out to you a single gate, to bring you back to the source. Do you still hear the cawing of crows and the chatter of magpies?” “I do.” “Then turn your hearing back upon your own hearing-nature. Are there still many sounds?” “When I arrive here, all sounds and all discriminations are entirely unobtainable.” “How wonderful! How wonderful! This is Avalokiteśvara’s gate of entering the principle. I ask you further: you say that when you arrive here, all sounds and all discriminations are entirely unobtainable. Since they are unobtainable, at that very moment—is it not emptiness?” “Originally it is not empty; it is clearly luminous, not dimmed.” “What then is the substance of the non-empty?” “It has no appearance either; it cannot be reached by words.” “This is the life-span of all the Buddhas and all the patriarchs; doubt it no more.” [One pure awareness (yījīngmíng)]Refers to the pure mind of self-nature originally possessed by every person. “Pure and subtle” describes its bright, clear, and wondrous quality. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: “Originally based upon a single pure awareness, it is divided into a sixfold union.” A single pure awareness is the one mind. The sixfold union is the union of the six faculties with the six objects: the eye with form, the ear with sound, the nose with fragrance, the tongue with taste, the body with touch, and the mind with dharmas.
Excerpted from Old Master Xuyun’s Letter on Chan.
I often lament that the Dharma door
(the Chan gate)
has fallen into decay, and that genuine teachers
(good and wise teachers)
are rarely heard of. Yet those who study are as plentiful as the hairs of an ox,
(a metaphor for very many)
while those who accomplish are like the horns of a rabbit
(a metaphor for not a single one)
—all because they themselves lack the eye and ear,
(that is, because their course of reasoning is not clear)

and have erred in their proper tuning. Therefore the ancient worthy said: to have people look into the huatou, one must put down the whole body, as if one were a corpse, solely raise this single thought and carry it into investigation, and arouse the doubt.
Doubt what? Since it is called the head of the word, it has long since fallen to the tail of the word. One must know that the true huatou
is to be investigated toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted
. Without distinguishing activity from stillness, thought after thought without interval,
this is called the doubt

(To investigate—without distinguishing activity from stillness, thought after thought without interval—toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted is called the doubt. Note: here “the doubt” is the doubt of looking into the huatou, whereas the “doubt” spoken of in the earlier section “The Huatou and the Doubt” is the doubt of investigating the tail of the word.)
Doubt on and doubt on, until it is beaten into a single mass.
(After the doubt is beaten into a single mass,)
turn the light back and shine upon it: who is it that doubts? After a long, long time, when the melon ripens the stem falls; suddenly one touches the nostrils with which one was born
(thoroughly seeing one’s own nature)
, not obtained from outside.

[Since it is called the head of the word, it has long since fallen to the tail of the word]To suppose that a sentence or a single character is the huatou is in fact already the tail of the word. In Master Xuyun’s Convenient Instructions · Chan Hall Instructions, Elder Master Xuyun said: “The so-called huatou is the very moment before a single thought arises; the moment a single thought arises, it has already become the tail of the word.” [The three stages of Chan practice]First,

investigate toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted, until the doubt is beaten into a single mass; second, turn the light back and shine upon it, asking who it is that doubts; third, (after a long, long time,) when the melon ripens the stem falls, thoroughly seeing one’s own nature.
Therefore the Eternal Patriarch
(Master Yongjia)

said: “In walking there is Chan, in sitting there is Chan; whether speaking or silent, in movement or in stillness, the essence is at ease.” Practicing thus, what difficulty is there? From where does the sickness arise? The so-called “wild mind” is nothing but the mixed poisons of the past. One does not know that beneath the Chan school even a single word is of no use, and that Buddha and demon are cut off alike.

[Mixed poisons]All views, mysterious sayings, and wondrous words. Master Hanshan said: “The method of using the mind is to single-mindedly raise the thought of the upward task; you must strike at the very place where the Buddhas and patriarchs have no place, and plant your heels firmly. Next, you must spit out all at once the views, mysterious sayings, and wondrous words in your breast, which are mixed poisons.” (Dream Roaming Collection · Instructions to the Chan Practitioner Shuanglunzhao). He also said: “This matter (seeing one’s nature and becoming Buddha) is originally possessed by every person, without any deficiency, complete and full. That it is not known in daily use and not received in benefit is precisely because the evil seeds of beginningless habitual tendencies have been accumulated over eons and deeply entrenched, so that they have long been hard to uproot. Now, newly refined with the words of teaching and letters, the gong’an (public cases) of the patriarchs, and views of every kind, an additional layer of obstruction is added. Though one seeks to be clear about oneself, the more one seeks the further one is. Why is this so? Only because, being blind to oneself, one seeks and takes from outside. Because the afflictions and habitual tendencies accumulated over many lives are called the affliction-obstruction, while mysterious views are called the knowledge-obstruction. If these two obstructions are eliminated, the essence itself is revealed. Now, in investigating the upward matter, first let go of the entire literary language, mysterious principles, and learning of the past, and name them mixed poisons, spitting them out utterly. Solely raise your own original huatou, lay down the doubt anew, and cut off the very root of idle thoughts and afflictions, so that within cannot come out and without cannot enter. When the boundary of before and after is cut, the middle is isolated of itself, and there is only a single ball of doubt as the very life-root of your own being. Doubt on until you can doubt no further, and at the place where no strength can be applied, gaze fixedly and see what after all it is. Looking and looking, pressing and pressing, there will of itself come a time when the matter collapses. But leave so much as a hair’s breadth of views in it, and you are separated by a thousand, ten thousand miles. Just look at the First Patriarch (Patriarch Bodhidharma), who said: ‘Making the mind like a wall, one may enter the Way’—this is the first road of returning home. If the mind is unwilling to die and the doubt is not to the point, then for a thousand lives and a hundred eons one will remain forever on the road. Abbot, just gather your spirit into this, and I assure you that, on the day of attainment, it will surely not be a place that the empty bookish phrases of “zhi, hu, zhe, ye” can reach. Strive with all your might!” (Dream Roaming Collection · Instructions to the Lay Abbot Zhixian) [Collapse (dàoduàn)]The conclusion. Here it means thoroughly seeing one’s own nature.

As for what is called activity and stillness, the beginner in study cannot but investigate it. Walking, standing, being in the hall, at work, receiving and seeing off guests, talking and laughing, urinating and defecating—these are called activity; sitting and lying down in quietness are called stillness. Examine it subtly in this way
(examine it subtly in this way)
: in the course of the six periods of the day and night
(in the course of my present twenty-four hours)
, at what time am I in activity without being carried off by activity
(still investigating toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted)
? At what time am I in stillness without being turned by stillness
(still investigating toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted)
? In the presence of all circumstances, does the mind arise or not arise? If one can examine as before
(if one truly can examine in this way)
, then in activity, not being carried off by activity
(not giving rise to delusive thoughts in activity)
, one can be alert and still
(alert and at the same time still)
; in stillness, not being turned by stillness
(in stillness, not sinking into drowsiness)
, one is still and alert
(quiet and at the same time alert)

This is merely the awakening of your beginner’s mind. In activity and stillness do not lean and wither to one side; be certain that activity and stillness are one suchness, with matter and principle wholly interfused. This is just what the Twenty-seventh Patriarch
(the Twenty-seventh Patriarch of the Western Heaven, the Venerable Prajñātāra, the teacher of Patriarch Bodhidharma)

said: “In the in-breath I do not dwell in the realms of the aggregates; the out-breath does not touch the many conditions; thus I ever turn such a sūtra—a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, koṭi rolls.”

[The realms of the aggregates (yīnjie)]The five aggregates and the eighteen realms. [Five aggregates (wǔyīn)]An older translation of the five skandhas; “yīn” carries the sense of veiling—it can veil the true reality of thusness and give rise to all afflictions. [Five skandhas]Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, the five great elements constituting the human person. The aggregate of form is the body; the four aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the mind. [Eighteen realms]The union of the six faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; the six objects of form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas; and the six consciousnesses of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—these together are called the “eighteen realms.”

[In the in-breath I do not dwell in the realms of the aggregates; the out-breath does not touch the many conditions]This is an instance of “mutual wording,” meaning: the in-breath (inhaling) and the out-breath (exhaling) are not deluded by body and mind, and the in-breath and the out-breath are not deluded by realms and conditions. In other words, at no time is one deluded by body and mind or by realms and conditions. [Mutual wording (hùwén)]Mutual wording, also called “mutual phrasing,” is a rhetorical device commonly used in Classical Chinese. Its characteristic is that it is neither verbose nor redundant nor flat and straightforward, but subtle and condensed, with the wording spare while the meaning is preserved; the two parts complement each other to reveal the sense and reflect off each other with radiance. For example, in the “Ballad of Mulan,” “generals die in a hundred battles, warriors return after ten years” means: generals and warriors die in a hundred battles, and generals and warriors return after ten years. Another example is in the “Record of the Yueyang Tower,” “not rejoicing over things, not grieving over oneself,” which means: not rejoicing because of things or self, and likewise not grieving because of things or self. Here “things” refers to people other than oneself and the circumstances in which one lives, while “self” refers to one’s personal lot.

[In the in-breath I do not dwell in the realms of the aggregates; the out-breath does not touch the many conditions; thus I ever turn such a sūtra—a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, koṭi rolls]The in-breath and the out-breath are not deluded by body and mind, are not deluded by realms and conditions; to ever recite such a sūtra (taking ultimate reality as the sūtra) is equivalent to reciting a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, koṭi rolls of sūtras. The “Congrong Record” says: “The king of Eastern India invited the Twenty-seventh Patriarch Prajñātāra. During the meal, the king asked: ‘Why do you not read the sūtras?’ The Patriarch said: ‘This poor monk’s in-breath does not dwell in the realms of the aggregates, and the out-breath does not touch the many conditions; thus I ever turn such a sūtra—a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, koṭi rolls.’” [Turning the sūtra]Reciting the sūtra. The “Biographies of Eminent Monks · On Sūtra Readers” says: “Chanting sūtras is called turning and reading; singing praise is called Sanskrit voice.” [During the meal (zhāicì)]At the table during the vegetarian feast. “Cì” carries the sense of “in the midst of,” as in “in the breast” (xiōngcì) and “at the table” (xícì).
Beyond thought and discussion
(one must not go about thinking and discussing; in Chan practice one must not use the mind of consciousness to ponder, conjecture, or argue)

. Never seek after words, turn with the tongue-roots of others, and exhaust one’s very spirit to no real benefit. Sitting on the rush cushion, one dozes and is dull; when one unbends the legs, one idly chatters. When one meets circumstances and sounds
(conditions)
, one has no mastery whatsoever. How bitter! Let each of you be careful.
Note: The “Old Master Xuyun’s Letter on Chan” was originally published in “Sound of the Sea Tide” (Haichao Yin), Year Ten, Issue Four, and should be
, a letter that Elder Master Xuyun wrote around that time to his disciple Master Xiuyuan, giving instructions on investigating the huatou.

blocks.text: The Two Kinds of Easiness and Difficulty in Practice

inline.s: For those who apply effort in the cultivation of the Way, in terms of the depth or shallowness of their practice, there are two kinds of easiness and difficulty: first, the easiness and difficulty of the beginner’s effort; second, the easiness and difficulty of the seasoned practitioner’s effort.

blocks.text: 1. The Easiness and Difficulty of the Beginner’s Effort

inline.s: [The thieving mind (tōuxīn)]The mind that grasps at conditions. Because this mind of grasping at conditions steals the Dharma-wealth, keeping the true Dharma from appearing, the Chan grove calls it the thieving mind. The “Anheidou Collection” says:
“While the thieving mind is not dead, it is the great affliction of the student.”

[The mind that grasps at conditions (pānyuánxīn)]The mind that arises by grasping at the six objects; it is also called the deliberating mind. [Dharma-wealth (fǎcái)]The counterpart of “worldly wealth,” referring to the Buddha-Dharma. Because the Buddha-Dharma can moisten and nourish sentient beings and is the provision for nurturing their wisdom-life, just as worldly treasure is, it is metaphorically called Dharma-wealth.

The common sickness of the beginner’s effort is that the habitual tendencies of idle thinking cannot be put down—ignorance and conceit, jealousy and obstruction, greed, hatred, delusion, and craving, idleness and a taste for fine food, right and wrong and self-and-others fill up a whole belly. How could such a one be in accord with the Way?
[Conceit (gònggāo)]Arrogance and self-importance.

Or there be one who comes of a family of pampered young gentlemen, whose old habits are not forgotten, who cannot endure the least grievance, who cannot bear the slightest hardship—how could such a one apply effort in the Way? He never considers what sort of person the original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha was when he left the home life.
Or there be some who have learned a few characters, yet do not understand that the questions in the recorded sayings of the ancient worthies are meant to test the depth or shallowness of the student
(to test the depth or shallowness of the student’s practice)

; so they fancy themselves clever, and all day long hunt for phrases and sentences, discoursing on mind and on Buddha, taking the words of the ancients as something to be understood and explained. Doing this business of talking about food and counting treasures, they still think themselves remarkable and give rise to great arrogance. When they meet a serious illness, they cry out in bitter distress; or when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives
(or when death arrives)
, they are flustered and confused. The knowledge and understanding of their whole life is of no use at all—only then do they regret it too late.
